                             P UBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS

                                                  Project No. 59142
                             Review of ERCOT's Interconnection Processes for Large Loads


                                 COMMENTS OF PALLARA, INC.

Pallara, Inc. respectfully submits these comments on Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc.’s Requests for
Good Cause Exceptions Relating to Batch Zero Deadlines and Status Update on Additional Matters
Including the Long-Term Load Forecast, filed in this project on August 10, 2026 as Item 42. ERCOT’s
request concerns the timelines established in Planning Guide Sections 5 and 9 and follows ERCOT Market
Notice M-A080326-01, issued August 3, 2026.

I. Interest of the commenter
Pallara, Inc. is a Texas-based software company that builds evidence-tracking systems for large-load
interconnection readiness. Pallara is not a market participant, does not represent any interconnection
applicant in this proceeding, and takes no position on the eligibility of any individual project. Pallara’s
interest is confined to the documentation mechanism at issue.

II. Position
Pallara supports granting the requested good cause exception.
ERCOT states in Market Notice M-A080326-01 that it “will not notify each Interconnecting Distribution
Service Provider and Transmission Service Provider of how any Large Load is classified in the Batch Zero
Interconnection Study by August 7, 2026,” and that the Governor has directed a verification process before
data center Large Loads advance through interconnection. Compressing a verification directive into an
unchanged notification deadline would force ERCOT to choose between the deadline and the verification.
Neither outcome serves reliability. The exception is the correct instrument.

III. The record describes a documentation-completeness failure, not a study-capacity failure
ERCOT’s July 29, 2026 presentation to the Texas Senate Committee on Business and Commerce sets out
preliminary Batch Zero eligibility on slide 10, with data as of July 28, 2026. The categories are stated in
ERCOT’s own terms:
C ATEGORY                                                                                                       P ROJECTS

Not included in Batch Zero — no qualifying study                                                                          315

Not included in Batch Zero — no dynamic model submitted to ERCOT by July 10                                                47

Eligible for inclusion as allocated load                                                                                  127

Eligible for inclusion, base or allocated load to be determined                                                            49

Eligible for inclusion as base load                                                                                       150

Total assessed (sum of the above)                                                                                         688




                               Comments of Pallara, Inc. · PUCT Project No. 59142 · Page 1 of 3
 Of the 688 large load projects assessed, 362 were preliminarily excluded on documentation grounds.
ERCOT’s stated key takeaway on the same slide reads: “Approximately 205 GW of Large Load is eligible
for inclusion in Batch Zero based on existing studies.”
The significant fact is what does not appear in that taxonomy. Not one exclusion category is a reliability
finding. Not one is a capacity constraint, a study result, or an engineering determination. Every project in
those two categories was removed because a required artifact was absent or was not received by a date.
The 47-project category is the more instructive of the two. Those projects had qualifying studies. They were
removed solely because a dynamic model did not reach ERCOT by July 10. That is not a technical deficiency
in the project. It is a failure of the submission record to be complete and legible on a date.
This distinction matters to the relief before the Commission. If the Batch Zero slip were a study-capacity
problem, more time would be the remedy and the exception would be a one-time accommodation. It is not a
study-capacity problem. It is a completeness problem, and completeness problems recur at every subsequent
gate unless the completeness state itself becomes something a party can check before the deadline rather than
discover after it. Batch One will present the same failure absent a change in how completeness is represented.

IV. Recommendation
Pallara recommends one narrow addition, appropriate for the exception order or for the process that follows
it:

        Require that each large-load interconnection submission carry a standardized, machine-
        readable completeness attestation that reports, per required artifact, (a) whether the
        artifact has been received, (b) the date of receipt, and (c) the specific revision of the
        governing requirement against which the artifact was evaluated.

Three properties do the work.
Per-artifact, not per-application. A binary “complete” or “incomplete” status tells an applicant nothing
actionable. A per-artifact status identifies the missing item while there is still time to supply it. The 47
projects removed for a missing dynamic model are precisely the population this addresses.
Machine-readable. The obligation runs across hundreds of projects, multiple distribution and transmission
service providers, and a Governor-directed verification. Completeness state that exists only in
correspondence and PDFs cannot be aggregated, audited, or reconciled at that scale. ERCOT, the
Commission, and the service providers should be able to compute the same completeness answer from the
same record without manual assembly.
Keyed to the requirement revision. This is the property most easily overlooked and it is the one that
prevents the next dispute. Large-load requirements have been revised materially and repeatedly, including
through NPRR1308 and NOGRR282. An artifact judged sufficient under one revision may be insufficient
under its successor. Absent a recorded revision reference, “we submitted that” and “that submission does not
qualify” are both true statements about the same document, and the disagreement is unresolvable from the
record. Recording the governing revision converts that dispute into a lookup.




                           Comments of Pallara, Inc. · PUCT Project No. 59142 · Page 2 of 3
 V. The recommendation is narrow and inexpensive
Pallara does not propose a new filing requirement, a new study obligation, a new fee, or a new deadline. The
attestation reports on artifacts already required. It creates no new substantive obligation for any applicant. It
changes only the form in which the completeness of existing obligations is represented, so that the
representation can be checked by the applicant before the deadline instead of adjudicated by ERCOT
afterward.
The verification the Governor has directed will require exactly this reconciliation across the queue.
Specifying the format once, now, is materially cheaper than reconstructing it per project during the
verification.

VI. Conclusion
Pallara supports the requested good cause exception. Pallara respectfully recommends that the Commission
direct or encourage ERCOT to adopt a standardized machine-readable per-artifact completeness attestation
carrying the governing requirement revision, so that the documentation failure evidenced in Batch Zero is not
repeated in Batch One.
Pallara appreciates the opportunity to comment.

Respectfully submitted,



Preston Jones
Founder
Pallara, Inc.
3723 Greenville Ave STE 35833
Dallas, TX 75206
preston@pallara.xyz

Dated: August 16, 2026
